transcript.text: Celeste, that's an important question and I don't want to over-promise. The honest answer is that a queenless colony getting a new queen by mid-May will need significant time to rebuild its population before it can produce surplus honey. We're looking at the queen being accepted by late May, then a couple weeks undisturbed as Ravi suggested, which puts us into mid-June before we can even assess the colony's strength. From mid-June to August 20th is roughly two months — that may or may not be enough for twelve jars plus adequate winter stores, depending on nectar flow and how quickly the colony rebounds. I think the responsible approach is to commit to the plan as we've outlined, but with a checkpoint around mid-June to honestly assess whether twelve jars is realistic. If it looks short, we should talk with the hospice fundraiser about what we can actually deliver rather than risking the colony's health or falling through on the commitment at the last minute. Does that approach work for everyone?

transcript.text: Nia, that sequencing makes perfect sense from a beekeeping perspective. Moving the hive is already stressful, and stacking that on top of queen introduction would significantly reduce her chances of being accepted. Here's what I'd recommend: move the hive to the far east fence first, ideally in the early evening when the foragers are back inside. Then give the colony at least three to five days to settle into the new location and reorient. After that, we introduce the new queen. That still keeps us well within the May 15th deadline, assuming we schedule the move for early May. The screened barrier can go up at the new location before or right after the move — it won't disturb the bees much since it's external to the hive itself. One more thing to flag: after a move, bees can be disoriented and may cluster around the old location for a day or two, so we should make sure the path between the patio and the new east fence site is clear during that transition period, especially given your neighbor's allergy concern.
